title: Android 12 to 16 behavior changes
scopeHtml: Scope: what changed per OS release, whether each change keys off targetSdk or the running OS, how to test it with compat flags, and how to bump targetSdk safely. Verified against developer.android.com behavior-change pages; anything not re-checked is marked "verify".

notes.title: targetSdk versus the OS version, and the bump playbook
notes.html:
The idea. Two numbers decide how your app behaves. The device's OS version (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT) says what the phone can do. Your targetSdkVersion says "I have tested my app against the rules of this version", so the OS keeps old, forgiving behaviour for you until you raise it.

Mechanism. The system applies many behaviour changes only when targetSdk >= N. These are "compat changes" (visible in adb shell am compat and Developer options > App Compatibility Changes, where you can toggle each one for testing). Changes that apply to all apps regardless of target (for example Doze rules, new permission dialogs for existing permissions on a newer OS) are listed in the "behavior changes: all apps" docs. Google Play also forces a minimum target: new apps and updates must target within one year of the latest release (for example API 34 by Aug 2024, API 35 by Aug 2025; confirm current dates in Play policy). compileSdk only decides which APIs you can compile against and is separate from both.

minSdk       : lowest OS you install on
targetSdk    : which behaviour rules you opted into
compileSdk   : which API surface you compile against (>= targetSdk)
SDK_INT      : the real OS at runtime -> use for branching

Playbook for a targetSdk bump under live traffic.

  1. Read "behavior changes: apps targeting N" and "all apps" lists. Make a checklist per area (FGS, alarms, permissions, intents, media, UI).
  2. Bump compileSdk first (no behaviour change), fix deprecations and build errors.
  3. Test on an emulator at the new API with App Compatibility toggles; run UI tests, Perfetto startup, and background-work scenarios (FCM, WorkManager, alarms, boot).
  4. Update libraries (Firebase, WorkManager, Play Core, ads SDKs) since they often carry their own manifest entries.
  5. Ship the bump in its own release, behind staged rollout (1%, 5%, 20%, 50%, 100%) while watching crash-free sessions, ANR rate and background-work success rate per OS version in Crashlytics / Play Console vitals.
  6. Keep the rollback path: a previous APK with the old targetSdk cannot always be reinstalled over a higher versionCode, so a hotfix is a new versionCode.

Industry examples. Large apps (Uber, Swiggy, Spotify) run a "targetSdk upgrade" project every year with a kill-switch per risky behaviour. Crashlytics keys like Build.VERSION.SDK_INT make regressions visible per OS.

Analogy. A driving test: the OS update is the road changing; the targetSdk is the rulebook edition you promise to follow. The traffic police are lenient with older rulebooks until you renew your licence.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying the targetSdk bump has no effect when the device already runs the new OS: many changes depend on the OS, many on the target.
  • Confusing compileSdk with targetSdk.
  • Bumping targetSdk in the same release as large feature work, so regressions cannot be isolated.

notes.title: android:exported on Android 12
notes.html:
The idea. A component with an intent filter used to be reachable by any app by default. That default was dangerous, so Android 12 makes you decide explicitly.

Mechanism. For targetSdk 31+, every Activity, Service and Receiver that has an <intent-filter> must declare android:exported="true|false", or the build/install fails (manifest merger error; installation fails with INSTALL_PARSE_FAILED_MANIFEST_MALFORMED). Before, the default was true if a filter existed and false otherwise. The launcher Activity needs exported="true". Libraries' components merge in and may lack the attribute, so the build error can point at a dependency; fix with a tools:node="merge" override or upgrade the library. Protect exported components with android:permission or check the caller; exported without protection lets any app start them (deep link injection, intent redirection).

<activity android:name=".DeepLinkActivity" android:exported="true">
    <intent-filter> ... </intent-filter>
</activity>
<service android:name=".SyncService" android:exported="false"/>

Industry examples. Firebase Messaging service, Facebook SDK activities and Branch/AppsFlyer deep link receivers were updated for Android 12 to ship the attribute. Security reports (Google Play's "Intent Redirection" warning) target exported components.

Analogy. A shop with a door onto the street: you now must say whether it is open to the public or staff only, rather than the shop guessing.

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking exported="false" blocks the system. The system and your own UID can still start it; PendingIntents you hand out also work.
  • Marking everything exported="true" to make the error go away.
  • Forgetting ContentProvider has its own exported/grantUriPermissions rules.

notes.title: PendingIntent mutability
notes.html:
The idea. A PendingIntent is a signed permission slip you give another app (the system, a notification, an alarm) to run something as you later. If the slip has blanks, the other party might fill them in maliciously.

Mechanism. For targetSdk 31+ you must pass FLAG_IMMUTABLE or FLAG_MUTABLE to PendingIntent.getActivity/getService/getBroadcast, otherwise it throws IllegalArgumentException: Targeting S+ ... requires that one of FLAG_IMMUTABLE or FLAG_MUTABLE be specified. Default to FLAG_IMMUTABLE. Use FLAG_MUTABLE only when something must fill in the intent: inline reply RemoteInput in notifications, bubbles, Geofence/location updates PendingIntents, and some media controls. Android 14 adds a rule: mutable PendingIntent with an implicit intent (no component) is blocked for targetSdk 34 (the base intent must be explicit). Android 14 also restricts apps from launching Activities from the background via PendingIntent unless opted in with ActivityOptions.setPendingIntentBackgroundActivityStartMode. Combine with FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT and distinct request codes, and make the intent identity differ with data/action (extras do not count for equality), otherwise two notifications share one PendingIntent and show the wrong content.

val pi = PendingIntent.getActivity(
    ctx, orderId.hashCode(), intent,
    PendingIntent.FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT or PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE)

Industry examples. WhatsApp inline reply uses a mutable PendingIntent; Android 12 crashes in apps using older Firebase/WorkManager/Glide-style libraries pointed to those libraries needing upgrades (WorkManager 2.7+ fixed its own PendingIntents).

Analogy. A cheque: a crossed, filled-in cheque (immutable) is safe; a blank cheque (mutable) is only for people you trust to fill in the amount.

Common interview traps.

  • Using FLAG_MUTABLE everywhere.
  • Same request code and action for different notifications, so taps open the wrong screen.
  • Believing extras make PendingIntents distinct. filterEquals ignores extras.

notes.title: Splash Screen API on Android 12
notes.html:
The idea. Every app now gets a system-drawn splash (app icon on a coloured background) while it starts. You may customise it, but you can no longer fake a full-screen custom splash Activity.

Mechanism. On API 31+ the system shows the splash for all apps automatically, using the launcher icon and windowBackground. Customise with the theme attributes windowSplashScreenBackground, windowSplashScreenAnimatedIcon, windowSplashScreenIconBackgroundColor, windowSplashScreenBrandingImage (not on all versions), and postSplashScreenTheme. The AndroidX androidx.core:core-splashscreen library backports the look to API 23+. Call installSplashScreen() before super.onCreate(). Hold it while loading with setKeepOnScreenCondition { viewModel.isLoading } (keep it very short; the guideline is under about a second) and animate exit with setOnExitAnimationListener. Old "SplashActivity with a 2 second delay" patterns produce a double splash on Android 12 and lengthen cold start.

Industry examples. Google's own apps and most large consumer apps use the system splash; some (Instagram, Spotify) keep it as brand icon on a flat colour. The splash window is created by StartingSurface in system_server before your process finishes forking, which is why it appears instantly.

Analogy. The restaurant's front door sign appears the moment you walk up, before the kitchen is even ready.

Common interview traps.

  • Keeping a delay-based SplashActivity, which causes a double splash and slower perceived start.
  • Using setKeepOnScreenCondition for network calls, effectively adding seconds of blank screen.
  • Calling installSplashScreen() after super.onCreate().

notes.title: Foreground service start restrictions (Android 12)
notes.html:
The idea. Apps in the background can no longer quietly turn themselves into foreground services. This stops hidden background work from hijacking the battery.

Mechanism. For targetSdk 31+ (and effectively for all apps in later versions), startForegroundService() from the background throws ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException (API 31+; on older versions it surfaces as IllegalStateException / RemoteServiceException ANR-type crash: "Context.startForegroundService() did not then call Service.startForeground()", which also appears if you forget to call startForeground() within about 5 seconds). Allowed exceptions include: app has a visible window, the app received a high-priority FCM message, was started from a notification action, exact alarm trigger (SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM/USE_EXACT_ALARM), BOOT_COMPLETED for some types (restricted again in 15), the user tapped something while the app was visible, an AccessibilityService or companion device event, and a few more. Alternatives: WorkManager expedited work (setExpedited, since 2.7) or setForegroundAsync inside a Worker.

Production incident. After a targetSdk 31 release, Crashlytics shows ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException from a JobService/BroadcastReceiver that started a music or tracking service on a scheduled trigger. Fix: schedule via an exact alarm or use WorkManager expedited; for user-initiated actions start from a visible UI; handle the exception, show a "tap to resume" notification instead.

Industry examples. Spotify and Uber start FGS while visible or from a user tap, and use FCM high-priority for "ride accepted" to re-enter allowed state. Apps like Zoom and Google Meet start FGS for ongoing calls from a visible incoming call UI.

Analogy. A shop assistant who is off shift cannot suddenly start serving customers; they must be called in by an allowed event.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing FCM always allows FGS start. Only high-priority messages do, and the budget depends on the app's standby bucket.
  • Forgetting to call startForeground within about 5 seconds.
  • Catching only IllegalStateException and missing the new exception class on API 31+.

notes.title: POST_NOTIFICATIONS and the rollout plan on Android 13
notes.html:
The idea. From Android 13, notifications need a runtime permission. The code is small; the product risk is large.

Mechanism. See the Permissions notes for the full flow. Key points for behaviour changes: targetSdk 33 apps must request it; apps below 33 get the system prompt auto-shown on first channel creation; existing installs upgraded from Android 12 keep their enabled state; the notification channel shows up in Settings regardless. NotificationManagerCompat.areNotificationsEnabled() works on all versions.

Rollout plan (ambiguous requirement and post-incident review). Typical incident: a team bumped targetSdk to 33, forgot the request, and push-driven re-engagement fell 40 percent among new installs, noticed only in weekly metrics. Remedy: (1) add analytics events for prompt shown, allowed, denied, permanently denied, and notification-enabled-state at session start; (2) define the trigger moments with product (after first order, after joining a group); (3) show a primer screen; (4) A/B test timing via Firebase Remote Config; (5) alert on opt-in rate and on push delivery per OS version; (6) add a "notifications are off" banner in settings with a Settings deep link (ACTION_APP_NOTIFICATION_SETTINGS).

Industry examples. Swiggy, Zomato and Uber delay the prompt until after an order or ride; news apps show a primer. Google recommends not asking at first launch.

Analogy. Asking someone for their phone number only after you have a reason to call.

Common interview traps.

  • Treating it as a pure code change with no analytics or rollout.
  • Forgetting existing users from earlier versions are grandfathered, so comparing opt-in between cohorts without segmentation misleads.
  • Prompting at launch.

notes.title: Media permissions on Android 13 and 14
notes.html:
The idea. Whole-library storage access is being replaced by "granular" and finally "selected photos only" access.

Mechanism. API 33 splits READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE into READ_MEDIA_IMAGES, READ_MEDIA_VIDEO, READ_MEDIA_AUDIO; on a 33+ device READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE is ignored for media. API 34 adds READ_MEDIA_VISUAL_USER_SELECTED and partial access (the user picks specific items; the grant lasts for the app session or until revoked). A manifest typically has:

<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE" android:maxSdkVersion="32"/>
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.READ_MEDIA_IMAGES"/>
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.READ_MEDIA_VISUAL_USER_SELECTED"/>

Best practice: use PickVisualMedia and avoid the permission entirely. Play restricts broad photo/video permissions to core-gallery use cases.

Industry examples. Gallery and file-manager apps keep permission; messaging and social apps use the picker; Google Photos uses full access.

Analogy. Letting a visitor see the whole photo album, only the shelf you choose, or only the photos you handed over.

Common interview traps.

  • Leaving only READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE, which stops working at API 33.
  • Not handling partial access (gallery looks empty or small).
  • Forgetting maxSdkVersion on the old permission.

notes.title: Per-app language and themed icons on Android 13
notes.html:
The idea. Users can choose a different language for each app, and monochrome icons can adopt the wallpaper colours.

Mechanism. Per-app language: declare res/xml/locales_config.xml with supported locales and reference it with android:localeConfig in the manifest; the system exposes it in Settings > System > Languages > App languages. Set it programmatically with LocaleManager.setApplicationLocales() (API 33) or the backport AppCompatDelegate.setApplicationLocales() (AppCompat 1.6+), which for API below 33 needs the AppLocalesMetadataHolderService entry with autoStoreLocales so choices persist. The locale change recreates Activities (config change). Themed icons: add <monochrome> to the adaptive icon (ic_launcher.xml), a single-colour vector; the launcher tints it (Pixel Launcher and similar).

Industry examples. WhatsApp, Google Maps and Netflix show up in per-app language; Indian apps (Paytm, PhonePe, Hotstar) with many regional languages benefit from localeConfig. Missing monochrome layers leave the icon un-themed on Pixel while others are tinted, which users notice.

Analogy. Each guest picks their own room language card instead of the whole hotel using one.

Common interview traps.

  • Hand-rolled locale code that conflicts with the system per-app setting.
  • Forgetting autoStoreLocales so the chosen language resets on older OS versions.
  • Shipping resources for a language but not listing it in locales_config.

notes.title: Foreground service types on Android 14
notes.html:
The idea. From Android 14 you must tell the system why your foreground service exists, in a fixed list of categories, and request the matching permission. This lets the system police abuse.

Mechanism. For targetSdk 34, every foreground service must declare android:foregroundServiceType in the manifest, plus the corresponding permission android.permission.FOREGROUND_SERVICE_<TYPE>, and pass the type to startForeground(id, notification, type) (or ServiceCompat.startForeground). Types include camera, connectedDevice, dataSync, health, location, mediaPlayback, mediaProjection, microphone, phoneCall, remoteMessaging, shortService, specialUse, systemExempted. Missing type or permission throws MissingForegroundServiceTypeException or SecurityException. Some types also need runtime conditions, for example location needs the app to already hold a location permission, camera/microphone need those runtime permissions, and starting a camera/microphone/location FGS from the background is restricted (while-in-use permission rules). specialUse requires a Play Console declaration; shortService runs about 3 minutes.

Spot-the-bug (targetSdk 34 bump). The service is declared with no type, startForeground(1, n) called with the two-argument form, and a manifest permission missing. On API 34 devices Crashlytics shows MissingForegroundServiceTypeException: Starting FGS without a type. Fix: declare android:foregroundServiceType="mediaPlayback" plus FOREGROUND_SERVICE_MEDIA_PLAYBACK, and call the 3-argument start with the same type.

Industry examples. Spotify/YouTube Music use mediaPlayback; Google Maps navigation uses location; Zoom uses microphone/camera/phoneCall; file sync apps used dataSync (which Android 15 limits).

Analogy. Entering a building: you now must say "delivery", "visitor" or "maintenance" and show the matching pass.

Common interview traps.

  • Declaring type in the manifest but not passing it in code (or vice versa).
  • Picking dataSync as the catch-all type.
  • Forgetting the type-specific permission.

notes.title: Exact alarms from Android 12 to 14
notes.html:
The idea. Exact alarms wake the phone at a precise second, which costs battery. Android gradually moved them behind a permission.

Mechanism. API 31: SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM introduced, granted by default for apps. API 33: USE_EXACT_ALARM for apps whose core function is alarm clock or calendar (granted at install, but Play-restricted). API 34: SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM is no longer pre-granted to newly installed apps targeting 33+ (confirm exact rules in docs); the user grants it in Settings > Alarms & reminders. Check AlarmManager.canScheduleExactAlarms(); without it setExact / setExactAndAllowWhileIdle throw SecurityException (setAlarmClock is a separate, user-visible route; confirm its exemption in the docs). Revocation by the user kills the app and cancels its alarms; listen to ACTION_SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM_PERMISSION_STATE_CHANGED to reschedule. Prefer inexact setAndAllowWhileIdle, WorkManager, or setWindow when exactness is not essential.

Production incident (denial on Android 14). A reminder app crashed with SecurityException: Caller needs to hold android.permission.SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM on new installs on API 33 and 34 devices, because the manifest declared the permission but code never checked canScheduleExactAlarms(). Fix: check, show an explanation with an intent to ACTION_REQUEST_SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM, fall back to inexact with a note, and reschedule on the state-changed broadcast.

Industry examples. Google Clock and Calendar use USE_EXACT_ALARM; medication-reminder and meeting apps need the user grant; delivery apps use FCM instead.

Analogy. A bell that rings at the exact second needs the building manager's approval because it wakes everyone.

Common interview traps.

  • Declaring the permission and assuming it is granted.
  • Using USE_EXACT_ALARM without being an alarm/calendar app (Play rejection).
  • Not rescheduling after permission change or reboot.

notes.title: Edge-to-edge on Android 15 and 16
notes.html:
The idea. Apps are expected to draw behind the status and navigation bars. Android 15 forces this for apps targeting 35; you handle the overlap yourself with insets.

Mechanism. For targetSdk 35 on Android 15 the window is edge-to-edge by default; android:windowOptOutEdgeToEdgeEnforcement is a temporary opt-out that is removed/ignored for apps targeting 36 on Android 16. Use enableEdgeToEdge() (activity 1.8.0+), ViewCompat.setOnApplyWindowInsetsListener, WindowInsetsCompat.Type.systemBars() and displayCutout(), ime() for the keyboard. In Compose use Scaffold content padding, WindowInsets.safeDrawing, Modifier.windowInsetsPadding, and imePadding(). Also, the status bar colour is ignored (transparent) and three-button navigation gets a translucent scrim; dialogs/bottom sheets/SearchBar need inset handling.

Symptoms. Toolbar hidden behind the status bar, buttons under the gesture bar, content under the keyboard, and double padding when both legacy fitsSystemWindows and new insets apply.

Industry examples. Google Maps, Gmail and YouTube already draw edge-to-edge; many XML-based apps had to migrate in 2025 to target 35.

Analogy. A painting extended to the edge of the wall: you now have to keep the important signature away from the frame yourself.

Common interview traps.

  • Applying insets twice (parent and child).
  • Ignoring IME insets.
  • Assuming statusBarColor still works on 15.

notes.title: Foreground service timeouts and boot restrictions on Android 15
notes.html:
The idea. The system no longer lets certain foreground services run forever, and it blocks some from being started at boot.

Mechanism. Android 15 (targetSdk 35) puts a time limit on dataSync and mediaProcessing foreground services: about 6 hours total in a rolling 24 hours (confirm in the docs). When the limit hits, the system calls Service.onTimeout(int startId, int fgsType) (API 35); the service has a few seconds to call stopSelf(), otherwise the system throws RemoteServiceException$ForegroundServiceDidNotStopInTimeException (a crash). Restarting is not allowed until the user brings the app to the foreground. Boot: apps cannot launch certain FGS types from a BOOT_COMPLETED receiver: dataSync, camera, mediaPlayback, phoneCall, mediaProjection, microphone throw ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException. location, connectedDevice etc. are still allowed if permission conditions hold.

Production incident (dataSync timeout crashes). A cloud-backup app used one long dataSync FGS for a first-time upload and crashed for many users at the 6-hour mark with ForegroundServiceDidNotStopInTimeException. Remedy: implement onTimeout() to save progress and stopSelf(); move long uploads to WorkManager with setForeground/user-initiated data transfer jobs (UIDT, API 34, setUserInitiated(true)) which has no such hard limit but shows a notification; checkpoint and resume; show "tap to continue".

Industry examples. Google Drive/Photos backup uses WorkManager-like jobs; Dropbox and OneDrive moved large transfers to user-initiated jobs.

Analogy. A parking meter that now stops automatically after 6 hours, and the parking lot closes its gates when you restart your car at night.

Common interview traps.

  • Not implementing onTimeout.
  • Starting a mediaPlayback FGS from BOOT_COMPLETED on Android 15.
  • Thinking the limit resets by restarting the service in the background.

notes.title: 16 KB page size
notes.html:
The idea. Memory is handed out in pages. Most phones used 4 KB pages; Android 15+ devices may use 16 KB, which speeds some things and saves RAM. Native libraries compiled assuming 4 KB break.

Mechanism. ELF .so files have LOAD segments aligned to a page boundary. If a library is aligned to 4 KB (p_align = 0x1000) the kernel with 16 KB pages cannot map it correctly; the app crashes at dlopen/loading with a native error, or the system shows a compatibility warning (Android 15 QPR / Android 16: a "not 16 KB compatible" dialog; Google Play requires 16 KB support for new apps and updates targeting Android 15+ from Nov 1, 2025; confirm the current deadline). Check with unzip + readelf -l lib.so | grep LOAD (alignment should be 0x4000 or higher), Android Studio APK Analyzer (it flags alignment), or check_elf_alignment.sh. Fix: AGP 8.5.1+ and NDK r28+ build 16 KB-aligned by default (NDK r27: pass -Wl,-z,max-page-size=16384); update third-party .so dependencies; zip alignment of uncompressed libs needs AGP 8.5.1 too (the APK/AAB must also be 16 KB zip-aligned). Test with the 16 KB emulator image or Developer options (16 KB mode on Pixel 8+ with Android 15 QPR1).

Readiness plan (design trade-off). Inventory all .so (including from SDKs like ML Kit, Mapbox, Unity, game engines, WebRTC, SQLCipher, Realm); ask vendors for compliant versions; add a CI step that fails on misaligned ELF; test on the emulator; decide whether to drop or replace non-updating SDKs; keep android:extractNativeLibs="false" in mind (affects how libraries are mapped).

Industry examples. Game and camera/ML-heavy apps (Unity games, TensorFlow Lite, Mapbox) were most affected in 2025.

Analogy. Moving boxes sized for a small shelf into a bigger shelf with bigger slots: boxes not made to fit the new slot size will jam.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing pure Kotlin/Java apps are unaffected even if they bundle an SDK with .so files.
  • Checking only your own native code.
  • Forgetting zip alignment of the package, not only ELF alignment.

notes.title: Predictive back
notes.html:
The idea. The back gesture now shows a preview of where you will land (home screen, previous screen) as you swipe. For that the system needs to know in advance whether your app will handle back, so old "intercept in onBackPressed" code stops working.

Mechanism. Opt in with android:enableOnBackInvokedCallback="true" (application or activity). KeyEvent.KEYCODE_BACK and onBackPressed() are not called when enabled on targetSdk 33+; use OnBackPressedCallback (AndroidX, addCallback(owner, callback), with isEnabled toggled) or OnBackInvokedDispatcher. Android 13 shows the back-to-home animation behind a developer option; Android 14 adds cross-activity and cross-task animations; Android 15 makes back-to-home on by default for apps that opt in. Material components (bottom sheets, side sheets, search bar) and Navigation Compose (PredictiveBackHandler, BackHandler) support progress callbacks. Fragments need Navigation/Fragment 1.6+ for animations.

Spot-the-bug. Override of onBackPressed() to show an "unsaved changes" dialog; on API 33+ with the flag, the dialog never shows and the app exits. Another: a callback registered with isEnabled = true always, which blocks back-to-home animation; enable it only when it has something to intercept. A third: using BackHandler inside a composable that leaves composition, leaving stale state.

Industry examples. Google Play Store, Settings and Gmail show the animation; many apps with custom back stacks (WebView, multi-pane) had to be reworked.

Analogy. A lift showing the next floor's preview as you press the button, so the lift must say in advance which floor it will stop at.

Common interview traps.

  • Leaving onBackPressed overrides in place.
  • A permanently enabled OnBackPressedCallback.
  • Doing real work (network calls, commits) inside the progress callback instead of on commit.

notes.title: Android 16 adaptive layouts and background work changes
notes.html:
The idea. Android 16 removes the escape hatches that let phone-only apps stay locked to portrait, and tightens background work again.

Mechanism: adaptive. For apps targeting SDK 36 on large screens (smallest width 600dp or more: tablets, foldables, desktop-windowing), the system ignores screenOrientation, resizeableActivity="false", and aspect-ratio restrictions (minAspectRatio, maxAspectRatio) and the app must handle resizing. Games (category) are exempt, and the user can opt out per app via settings. Use window size classes (WindowSizeClass), ListDetailPaneScaffold, NavigationSuiteScaffold, and the Jetpack WindowManager library; do not use Configuration.orientation or Display size as a proxy for device type. Test with the resizable emulator.

Mechanism: background work (Android 16). Job quotas are tightened and tied to the app's standby bucket and whether it recently ran a foreground service; the system also considers the reason a job was stopped (STOP_REASON_*) and JobScheduler.getPendingJobReasons() lets you see why a job has not run. Exact alarm quotas and JobInfo behaviours changed, and some 16 releases add stricter limits on jobs started while the app is not in the top state (confirm details in the Android 16 behavior-change docs, since this area evolves). Also in 16: the edge-to-edge opt-out ends, and predictive back is enabled by default for targetSdk 36.

Industry examples. Instagram, Netflix and banking apps historically locked portrait; the Play Store large-screen quality rules and Google's tablet push drive migration.

Analogy. A shop that was only allowed to display goods in one size of window; now the window can be any size and the shop must rearrange the display.

Common interview traps.

  • Using orientation checks as a tablet check.
  • Assuming the manifest orientation lock still works on large screens.
  • Not testing background jobs after the quota changes; use adb shell cmd jobscheduler and getPendingJobReasons.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• targetSdk opts you into new rules; the OS version decides what exists. Bump in its own release, staged, with a checklist.
  • Android 12: android:exported, PendingIntent mutability, system splash screen, FGS background-start ban, exact alarm permission.
  • Android 13: POST_NOTIFICATIONS, granular media permissions, per-app language, themed icons, opt-in predictive back.
  • Android 14: FGS types and permissions, partial photo access, exact alarms denied by default, tighter PendingIntent rules.
  • Android 15: edge-to-edge enforced, dataSync/mediaProcessing FGS timeouts via onTimeout, boot-time FGS restrictions, 16 KB pages.
  • Android 16: adaptive layouts on large screens, edge-to-edge opt-out removed, predictive back default, tighter background job quotas.
  • Always plan: read behaviour-change docs, test with compat toggles, stage rollout, watch vitals per OS version.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between compileSdk, targetSdk and minSdk, and how do you know whether a given Android behavior change hits your app only after you bump targetSdk or immediately when users update their OS?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Every "app broke after OS update" incident starts here. Seniors can predict blast radius before shipping.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: minSdk is the oldest OS I install on, compileSdk is the SDK I compile against (APIs and lint), targetSdk is the OS version I promise my app was tested against. The platform gates many behavior changes on targetSdk, so they only turn on when I bump it. The rest apply to every app on that OS version regardless of targetSdk. Google publishes both lists per release: "Behavior changes: apps targeting API X" and "Behavior changes: all apps".

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism: the platform has a compat framework. Each behavior change is a named ChangeId (for example REQUIRE_EXACT_ALARM_PERMISSION, FGS_INTRODUCE_TIME_LIMITS). A change is either:

  • Gated on a targetSdk threshold: enabled only if app.targetSdk >= N and the device runs OS >= N.
  • Ungated (all apps): enabled for everyone on that OS.
  • Opt-in/debug: off by default, toggleable for testing.
                 device OS 15 (API 35)
app targetSdk 33 ----> all-apps changes for 15 ON, targeting-35 changes OFF (legacy compat)
app targetSdk 35 ----> all-apps changes ON, targeting-35 changes ON

Two consequences. First, the gate needs both conditions: targeting 35 on an Android 14 device gets no 35 behavior (mostly; some are library-backed). Second, a gate is time-limited: Play requires a recent targetSdk, and for some changes the opt-out is explicitly temporary (Android 16 large-screen restrictions opt-out "won't apply when targeting API 37").

How to know: (1) read the two pages for the release; (2) adb shell am compat toggles (see Q330); (3) lint (NewApi, UnspecifiedImmutableFlag, ExportedReceiver); (4) run on a new-OS device with the old targetSdk and with the new targetSdk, diff behavior.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// build.gradle.kts
android {
    compileSdk = 36          // lets me call new APIs, surfaces new lint; changes no runtime behavior
    defaultConfig {
        minSdk = 26          // install floor
        targetSdk = 35       // opt-in switch for "targeting N" behavior changes
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "I did not change targetSdk so I am safe." All-apps changes (Android 16 ordered-broadcast priority scope, JobScheduler quota, 16 KB compat dialog) hit you anyway.
  • Bumping compileSdk and assuming runtime behavior changed. It does not; only APIs and lint do.
  • Forgetting libraries: AndroidX or an SDK may check Build.VERSION.SDK_INT, not targetSdk, and change behavior on their own.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can compileSdk be lower than targetSdk? → AGP warns/errors; you cannot meaningfully target an SDK you do not compile against. Keep compileSdk >= targetSdk.
  2. Why does Play force targetSdk upgrades? → To stop apps from staying in legacy-compat mode with weaker security/privacy. Exact deadlines change yearly, so check Play Console help (verify).
  3. A change is in the "all apps" list but the doc says "on some releases". What does that mean? → Behavior can differ by QPR/OEM build; test on a real target device rather than trusting only emulator images.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE defines the three numbers. Senior explains the ChangeId gate, that both OS and targetSdk must match, that all-apps changes ignore targetSdk, and uses compat flags plus the two docs pages as a release-readiness checklist.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team bumped only compileSdk and thought the release was "safe", then an Android 16 OTA changed broadcast ordering across their two processes and a priority-dependent receiver chain broke. It was an all-apps change; targetSdk was never involved.

questions.promptHtml: What changed about android:exported in Android 12, what happens if you ignore it, and how do you decide the value for each component?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the first hard build break people hit on a targetSdk 31 bump and it is a real attack surface question.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: For apps targeting API 31+, any activity, service or receiver that has an intent filter must declare android:exported explicitly. If missing, manifest merge fails at build time (or the install fails on old tooling). Launcher activities must be true. Everything internal should be false. Exported means other apps can start or bind the component, so each true is public API plus an attack surface.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Before 31 the default was implicit: a component with an intent filter was exported by default, one without was not. That silent default caused many accidental exposures (e.g. a deep-link handling activity that also accepted privileged extras). API 31 removes the default for components with filters. Providers were already explicit since API 17 targeting.

Decision rule:

Component exported
LAUNCHER activity true (required)
Deep link / App Link activity true (BROWSABLE from browser), validate every extra
Internal service/receiver with filter false, and prefer explicit intents
System broadcast receiver (BOOT_COMPLETED, etc.) true is needed for system delivery for manifest receivers declared for system broadcasts (verify per action); guard with permission
Exported + sensitive add android:permission with signature protection

Library manifests merge into yours. An SDK that forgot exported breaks your build after the bump, and you fix it with a tools:node="merge" override in your manifest.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
<activity android:name=".MainActivity" android:exported="true">
    <intent-filter>
        <action android:name="android.intent.action.MAIN"/>
        <category android:name="android.intent.category.LAUNCHER"/>
    </intent-filter>
</activity>

<service android:name=".SyncService" android:exported="false">
    <intent-filter><action android:name="com.example.START_SYNC"/></intent-filter>
</service>

Build error you see: Apps targeting Android 12 and higher are required to specify an explicit value for android:exported when the corresponding component has an intent filter defined.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Setting everything to true to make the error go away. That is a security regression.
  • Exported component trusting its Intent extras (intent redirection). Validate or use getParcelableExtra with class typing.
  • Assuming exported=false blocks the system: it blocks other apps, not the same UID or system as applicable.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. A third-party SDK activity lacks exported. How do you fix it without forking? → Override in your own manifest with tools:node="merge" and set the attribute; file a bug upstream.
  2. What does targetSdk 34 add on top? → Implicit intents are only delivered to exported components, so an implicit intent to your own exported=false activity fails (see Q314).
  3. How do you audit exposure? → adb shell dumpsys package <pkg> for exported components, lint, and aapt dump xmltree/merged manifest view in Studio.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "add the attribute". Senior ties it to attack surface, explains the pre-31 implicit default, uses signature permissions for exported-but-sensitive components, and audits the merged manifest.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A deep-link activity exported for marketing links also accepted an EXTRA_NEXT_INTENT and launched it, giving other apps a path into non-exported screens. Fixing exported alone did not help; extras validation did.

questions.promptHtml: Explain PendingIntent mutability requirements across Android 12 and 14. When do you actually need FLAG_MUTABLE, and what breaks if you use it wrong?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests security understanding (a PendingIntent is a signed capability) and real migration experience.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Targeting API 31+, every PendingIntent must specify FLAG_IMMUTABLE or FLAG_MUTABLE, else IllegalArgumentException. I default to immutable. Mutable is needed only when the receiver of the PendingIntent must fill in extras, like inline-reply notification actions or bubbles. Targeting API 34+, a mutable PendingIntent whose base Intent has no component or package (an implicit one) throws.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A PendingIntent is a token that lets another process (system UI, alarm manager, a notification) fire an Intent with your identity and permissions. If it is mutable and the base Intent is incomplete, whoever holds it can fillIn() the action, component, data, and redirect it. That is the classic PendingIntent hijack.

Rules:

  • API 31: flag required (lint UnspecifiedImmutableFlag). FLAG_IMMUTABLE exists since API 23.
  • API 34: mutable + implicit base intent = exception. Fix by making the base intent explicit (setComponent/setPackage) or switch to immutable.
  • Identity of a PendingIntent is (requestCode, Intent filterEquals on action/data/type/class/categories, not extras), so two PendingIntents that differ only in extras collide unless you vary requestCode or use FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT/FLAG_CANCEL_CURRENT.

When mutable is legitimate: RemoteInput direct reply (system must add the reply into the intent), some media/bubble metadata. On API 31+, remember the result of a mutable PI for RemoteInput must carry an explicit component.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val intent = Intent(context, ReplyReceiver::class.java) // explicit
val flags = PendingIntent.FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT or
    (if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 31) PendingIntent.FLAG_MUTABLE else 0) // needed for RemoteInput
val replyPi = PendingIntent.getBroadcast(context, 1, intent, flags)

val openPi = PendingIntent.getActivity(
    context, 0, Intent(context, MainActivity::class.java),
    PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE or PendingIntent.FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT
)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using FLAG_MUTABLE "because it used to work". Silent security hole.
  • Different extras, same requestCode, no UPDATE_CURRENT: notification actions fire with stale extras.
  • Reusing a cancelled PendingIntent from a stale alarm after app update.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not always mutable? → It is a redirect primitive; attacker fills in a new component.
  2. FLAG_NO_CREATE? → Returns null if none exists; use to check whether an alarm PI is already scheduled.
  3. Android 15 PendingIntent changes? → PendingIntent creators block background activity launches by default; the sender must opt in (ActivityOptions.setPendingIntentBackgroundActivityStartMode) and creator must allow it, see 15 secured BAL list.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE adds FLAG_IMMUTABLE. Senior explains the fill-in attack, knows the 34 implicit-mutable rule, PendingIntent identity rules, and the background-activity-launch opt-ins.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After a 31 bump, a reply-from-notification feature stopped delivering text: someone "fixed" the crash with FLAG_IMMUTABLE, so the system could not attach the RemoteInput result.

questions.promptHtml: What happened to splash screens in Android 12, and how do you implement one correctly for all API levels?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Almost everyone had a custom splash Activity. Interviewers see if you understand the system now owns app start.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: From Android 12 the system always draws a splash screen on cold and warm starts, built from your theme (window background color plus app icon). Custom splash Activities now show a double splash on 12+. The fix is androidx.core:core-splashscreen: set a splash theme, call installSplashScreen() before super.onCreate(), optionally hold it with setKeepOnScreenCondition.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The splash is shown by the system (Window/StartingWindow in WindowManager Shell) before your process draws. It is not your Activity; it exists to cover process start + first frame. If you have a SplashActivity, 12+ shows system splash, then your splash, then main: three transitions.

Design: theme Theme.SplashScreen with attributes windowSplashScreenBackground, windowSplashScreenAnimatedIcon, postSplashScreenTheme. The library backports behavior to API 21+. Android 12 also lets the app keep the splash up while the first screen loads via a pre-draw hook; on pre-12 the library mimics it.

Numbers (verify on the splash screen guide): icon is drawn in a circle mask; with icon background the icon area is 240dp inside a 160dp circle, without it 288dp inside a 192dp circle; animated icon max duration is about 1000ms.

Do not use the keep-on-screen hook for network waits: you are extending a blocking cold-start experience. Use it for cheap local state (theme, session) only.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
<style name="Theme.App.Starting" parent="Theme.SplashScreen">
    <item name="windowSplashScreenBackground">@color/brand</item>
    <item name="windowSplashScreenAnimatedIcon">@drawable/ic_launcher_foreground</item>
    <item name="postSplashScreenTheme">@style/Theme.App</item>
</style>
class MainActivity : ComponentActivity() {
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        val splash = installSplashScreen()   // before super.onCreate
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        splash.setKeepOnScreenCondition { !viewModel.isReady.value }
    }
}

Manifest: android:theme="@style/Theme.App.Starting" on the application or launch activity.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Keeping a SplashActivity with Thread.sleep/delay. Artificial startup latency and a double splash.
  • Calling installSplashScreen() after super.onCreate(): theme not switched.
  • Keeping the splash while awaiting a network call: users see the logo for 5s; Play vitals counts it as slow start.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if the app targets below 31? → The system still shows its default splash on 12+ (icon on windowBackground); verify exact legacy behavior on the guide.
  2. How do you animate the exit? → setOnExitAnimationListener gives a SplashScreenViewProvider; remove it when done.
  3. Interaction with edge-to-edge on 15? → Old core-splashscreen with SHORT_EDGES cutout mode could crash at launch on 15; docs say upgrade to 1.2.0-alpha01+ or set cutout mode ALWAYS.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE migrates to the library. Senior explains that the splash is a system starting window covering process start, measures cold start impact, and refuses to use it as a loading screen.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: App kept a 1.5s SplashActivity plus the 12 system splash; start-to-interactive regressed on Android 12 only and the team blamed the OS until they saw the duplicated transition in a trace.

questions.contextHtml: A ride-tracking app (900k DAU, 70 percent on Android 12 to 14) starts a location foreground service from an FCM data message handler so drivers resume tracking after reconnect. Last week Crashlytics shows a new top crash on Android 12+: android.app.ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException: startForegroundService() not allowed due to mAllowStartForeground false: service com.example/.TrackingService, 0.6 percent of sessions, only when the app was swiped away or idle for hours. Release 5.14 changed the FCM priority from high to normal to save battery. Android 11 and below show nothing. The code was untouched in the same period.
questions.promptHtml: Find the cause, stop the bleeding, and design the long-term fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Wrap it in try/catch" or "ask users to disable battery optimization". The crash disappears but tracking silently stops, and battery optimization is not an exemption from the rule.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did the stack come from startForegroundService in a receiver/FirebaseMessagingService? (confirms start path.) What is the FCM priority actually delivered? (the exemption depends on it.) Which targetSdk? Is ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION involved? Is this tied to the 5.14 server change only?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Server-side flip FCM back to high priority for tracking messages, and catch ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException (API 31+) to avoid crashes while we ship the real fix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) normal-priority FCM does not give the "high-priority message" FGS exemption; (b) service started from a receiver after the app was in a cached state; (c) the start used startService on a path that later promotes; (d) OEM aggressive kill (red herring, since the exception is a platform policy, not a kill).
  4. How I'd verify each: Log RemoteMessage.priority vs originalPriority in onMessageReceived; adb shell dumpsys activity services <pkg> and dumpsys deviceidle to see the app's standby bucket; reproduce with adb shell am kill or am force-stop then send test messages with priority normal/high; compare on an Android 11 device (no exception) to confirm a platform gate.
  5. Root cause: Starting a foreground service from the background (Android 12 rule) needs an exemption. Docs list exemptions such as visible app transition, a high-priority FCM message, notification action tap, exact alarm, and BOOT_COMPLETED (restricted further in 15). Normal-priority FCM is not an exemption, so on 12+ the platform throws. On 11 the same call worked.
  6. Fix: Short term: high priority for user-visible tracking pushes. Long term: do not start a location FGS on a push at all unless the user requested tracking. Use WorkManager expedited work with OutOfQuotaPolicy.RUN_AS_NON_EXPEDITED_WORK_WHEN_OUT_OF_QUOTA for short work, and let the foreground UI start the FGS when the user opens the app. For a legitimately ongoing trip, start the FGS from a user-visible action (notification action PendingIntent, or app foreground) and keep it alive instead of restarting on push.
try {
    ContextCompat.startForegroundService(ctx, Intent(ctx, TrackingService::class.java))
} catch (e: ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException) { // API 31+
    WorkManager.getInstance(ctx).enqueue(
        OneTimeWorkRequestBuilder<ResumeTrackingWorker>()
            .setExpedited(OutOfQuotaPolicy.RUN_AS_NON_EXPEDITED_WORK_WHEN_OUT_OF_QUOTA).build())
}
  1. Prevention: Test matrix includes "app killed, normal FCM" on 12, 13, 14; Crashlytics custom key for FCM priority; a server-side check so tracking pushes cannot be downgraded; lint/review rule: no startForegroundService in receivers/FCM without exemption comment.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not "just try/catch" (silently loses tracking), not asking for SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW as a workaround (policy and 15 narrowed that exemption), not moving to exact alarms to dodge the rule (abuse and permission denied by default on 14, see Q320).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• High priority FCM but the app is in a restricted standby bucket? → Priority can be downgraded for apps that don't show user-visible notifications; Android may demote high-priority messages if the app does not post notifications in response (verify FCM docs).
  • Android 15, BOOT_COMPLETED start of a location FGS? → Location type is not in the blocked list (dataSync, camera, mediaPlayback, phoneCall, mediaProjection, microphone), but still needs a legit exemption path.
  • Would WorkManager expedited work work on 11? → Yes, it falls back to a foreground service pre-12 inside WorkManager.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "battery saving" server tweak downgraded all pushes to normal priority on a Friday. The weekend crash graph looked like an OS rollout. The giveaway was the 11-vs-12 split and one log line for the priority flag.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: catches the exception; blames OEM or battery optimization.
  • Hire: identifies the FGS background start rule and the FCM priority exemption, restores high priority.
  • Strong hire: redesigns around user-initiated start, expedited work, instrumentation, and server guardrails; knows the 15 changes.

questions.contextHtml:
After bumping targetSdk from 33 to 34, QA reports three issues on Android 14 only: (1) pressing a notification action closes the app silently; (2) opening Settings from an in-app link does nothing; (3) the app crashes on cold start for some users with SecurityException: ... One of RECEIVER_EXPORTED or RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED should be specified when a receiver isn't being registered exclusively for system broadcasts. Code:

// Application.onCreate
registerReceiver(syncReceiver, IntentFilter("com.example.SYNC_DONE"))

// opening an internal screen
startActivity(Intent("com.example.OPEN_SETTINGS"))   // manifest: exported=false, has intent filter

// notification action
val i = Intent("com.example.REPLY")
val pi = PendingIntent.getBroadcast(this, 0, i, PendingIntent.FLAG_MUTABLE)
questions.promptHtml: Find every bug, explain which is targetSdk-gated, and fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Fixes only the crash from the stack trace and says the others are "OEM weirdness".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the same build behave on Android 13? (confirms 34 gating.) Do the 3 failures happen with targetSdk 33 on a 14 device? Is SYNC_DONE sent by our own process only?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not applicable beyond reverting the target bump; I would rather fix forward since the bumps are small and mechanical.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Three independent API-34 gates, each documented under "apps targeting 14": runtime receiver flag, implicit intent to non-exported component, mutable implicit PendingIntent.
  4. How I'd verify each: Logcat for the SecurityException and ActivityNotFoundException; lint; flip the compat change off via adb shell am compat disable <CHANGE> <pkg> where available, or compare against the 33-targeted build.
  5. Root cause:
    • Bug 1: a non-system broadcast needs RECEIVER_EXPORTED or RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED (34+). The action is ours, so it is not an "only system broadcasts" registration.
    • Bug 2: implicit intents are delivered only to exported components for 34+. Intent has no package, component is not exported, so resolution fails with ActivityNotFoundException.
    • Bug 3: mutable PendingIntent with an intent that has no component/package throws on 34+ (the "closes silently" symptom came from the crash being swallowed in a receiver chain).
  6. Fix:
ContextCompat.registerReceiver(this, syncReceiver, IntentFilter("com.example.SYNC_DONE"),
    ContextCompat.RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED)

startActivity(Intent(this, SettingsActivity::class.java))          // explicit; or setPackage(packageName)

val i = Intent(this, ReplyReceiver::class.java).setAction("com.example.REPLY") // explicit
val pi = PendingIntent.getBroadcast(this, 0, i,
    PendingIntent.FLAG_MUTABLE or PendingIntent.FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT) // mutable only if RemoteInput needs it
  1. Prevention: Lint errors-as-warnings: UnspecifiedRegisterReceiverFlag, UnspecifiedImmutableFlag; a "targetSdk bump" checklist (Q330); instrumented smoke tests on an API 34 emulator; review rule "internal intents are explicit".
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not marking components exported to make implicit intents work, which widens the attack surface.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does ContextCompat.registerReceiver help? → It adds the flag handling and, for non-exported on older APIs, a permission-based guard. Use it for backward compatibility.
  • A receiver registered only for ACTION_SCREEN_ON? → System-only broadcasts must not pass the flag per the docs; passing none is the documented exception.
  • Does targeting 34 also change JobScheduler? → Yes, long onStartJob/onStopJob callbacks on the main thread cause an ANR, and ACCESS_NETWORK_STATE is required if you set a network constraint.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Three fixes landed over two releases because each crash masked the next. Reading the whole behavior-changes page once up front would have found all three.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: fixes only the SecurityException.
  • Hire: finds all three and knows they are 34-gated.
  • Strong hire: also proposes lint config, test coverage and warns about the JobScheduler ANR change.

questions.promptHtml: How does the Android 13 notification runtime permission work, and does it behave differently depending on targetSdk?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It touched every app. The nuance (targetSdk, channels, foreground services, denial handling) separates people who shipped it from people who read the headline.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: POST_NOTIFICATIONS is a runtime permission on API 33+. If I target 33+, I declare it and request it myself at a good moment. If I target 32 or lower and run on Android 13, the system asks on my behalf the first time the app creates a notification channel (while an activity is in the foreground), so I lose control over timing. Denied means no notifications, including the foreground service notification in the drawer, but FGS still shows in the Task Manager.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Permission group: Notifications. Normal "dangerous" flow: checkSelfPermission -> shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale -> request via ActivityResultContracts.RequestPermission.
  • Apps updating from <33: existing installs are grandfathered as allowed when the user updates the OS (verify exact upgrade rule on the notification permission page).
  • Two denials (system dialog "Don't allow" twice) make it permanent; after that only Settings can change it. NotificationManagerCompat.areNotificationsEnabled() is the practical check since it also covers channel-level and app-level toggles.
  • Foreground services: the service still runs, but the user does not see the notification in the shade; the system exposes running FGS apps in the FGS Task Manager (API 33).
  • Exempt categories exist (media sessions, some system-granted) but do not rely on them.

Product design rule: do not ask at first launch. Ask in context (user follows an order, enables a reminder), explain the value first with a pre-permission screen, and measure opt-in rate.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val launcher = registerForActivityResult(ActivityResultContracts.RequestPermission()) { granted ->
    viewModel.onNotifPermissionResult(granted)
}

fun ensureNotifPermission() {
    if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 33) {
        when {
            ContextCompat.checkSelfPermission(this, Manifest.permission.POST_NOTIFICATIONS)
                == PackageManager.PERMISSION_GRANTED -> proceed()
            shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale(Manifest.permission.POST_NOTIFICATIONS) -> showRationale()
            else -> launcher.launch(Manifest.permission.POST_NOTIFICATIONS)
        }
    } else proceed()
}
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.POST_NOTIFICATIONS"/>

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Requesting on the splash. Opt-in drops; users reflexively deny and then it is permanently denied after a second deny.
  • Creating channels at Application.onCreate on a target-32 app: the system prompt triggers at an arbitrary moment (verify when exactly).
  • Treating granted == false as "never ask again" forever without a Settings deep link (Settings.ACTION_APP_NOTIFICATION_SETTINGS).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you test? → Fresh install on 13+, adb shell pm revoke <pkg> android.permission.POST_NOTIFICATIONS, and pm grant.
  2. Can a service notification be shown with the permission denied? → The FGS runs; notification is hidden in the drawer, visible in Task Manager.
  3. Do channels still matter? → Yes. Importance and per-channel toggles still apply; permission is the master switch.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE shows the permission code. Senior covers the targetSdk difference, grandfathering, FGS interplay, permanent denial, funnel measurement and where to ask.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team asked on first launch to "seed" opt-in; denial rate exceeded 60 percent and reactivation campaigns lost reach. Moving the ask after the first successful order recovered the funnel (see Q318).

questions.promptHtml: How did media access permissions change in Android 13 and 14, and what is the right architecture for picking photos today?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Storage permission questions reveal whether a candidate has followed the privacy direction of the platform.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Android 13 (targeting 33+) replaced READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE for media with READ_MEDIA_IMAGES, READ_MEDIA_VIDEO, READ_MEDIA_AUDIO. Android 14 (targeting 34+) added READ_MEDIA_VISUAL_USER_SELECTED so the user can grant "selected photos only". The best design is not to ask at all: use the system Photo Picker (PickVisualMedia), which needs no permission.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• API 33: three granular permissions. If a user previously granted READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE, READ_MEDIA_* are auto-granted on upgrade. Requesting images and video together shows one dialog.
  • API 34: with READ_MEDIA_IMAGES/VIDEO plus READ_MEDIA_VISUAL_USER_SELECTED declared, the dialog offers "Select photos and videos" vs "Allow all". If the user chooses partial, you get a grant of READ_MEDIA_VISUAL_USER_SELECTED only. Apps targeting <34 run in compat mode (the picker appears but the app sees the selection as a full grant of what was selected).
  • Granted state can be partial and can change while the app runs; the user can edit selection in Settings. Your queries to MediaStore must tolerate empty results.
  • Android 16 addition (targeting 36): app-owned photos are pre-selected in the limited-access picker; deselecting revokes your access to your own photos.

Architecture: ActivityResultContracts.PickVisualMedia (backported through Google Play services photo picker to API 19+ with androidx.activity 1.7+; verify minimum). Persist the returned Uri via takePersistableUriPermission only if the contract supports it, otherwise copy to app storage.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val pick = registerForActivityResult(ActivityResultContracts.PickVisualMedia()) { uri ->
    uri?.let { viewModel.onImagePicked(it) }
}
pick.launch(PickVisualMediaRequest(ActivityResultContracts.PickVisualMedia.ImageOnly))
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.READ_MEDIA_IMAGES"/>
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.READ_MEDIA_VISUAL_USER_SELECTED"/>
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE" android:maxSdkVersion="32"/>

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating "READ_MEDIA_IMAGES not granted" as "no access" when READ_MEDIA_VISUAL_USER_SELECTED is granted.
  • Not declaring READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE with maxSdkVersion=32, which leaves 12L and below broken.
  • Caching media Uris forever: with partial access, URIs can become invalid when the user edits selection.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does a gallery app need these permissions? → Yes, its job is broad access; Play also restricts READ_MEDIA_IMAGES/VIDEO use to core functionality (verify policy).
  2. How do you detect partial access? → Check granted state for READ_MEDIA_VISUAL_USER_SELECTED while images/video are not granted.
  3. Camera app writing its own photos? → Use MediaStore insert; no read permission needed for your own files.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE swaps permission names. Senior moves to the Photo Picker, handles partial grants and URI lifetime, and mentions Play policy risk for broad media permissions.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After a 34 bump, users who chose "select photos" saw an empty gallery tab because the code only checked READ_MEDIA_IMAGES. Support tickets said "the app lost my photos".

questions.promptHtml: What are per-app language preferences and themed icons in Android 13, and what does an app have to do to support them?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks if you know the small platform APIs that influence real UX and i18n architecture (and what "locale" means for Activity recreation).

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Per-app language lets the user pick a language for my app in system Settings, different from the system language. To support it I declare android:localeConfig pointing to an XML of supported locales (target 33+), and I use AppCompatDelegate.setApplicationLocales for pre-33 backport. Themed icons are a monochrome layer in the adaptive icon, which the launcher tints with the wallpaper palette.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Per-app language:

  • Framework API: LocaleManager.setApplicationLocales(LocaleList) on API 33+. AndroidX backport: AppCompatDelegate.setApplicationLocales(LocaleListCompat); for pre-33 devices persist the choice with AppLocalesMetadataHolderService (autoStoreLocales) in the manifest.
  • Manifest: android:localeConfig="@xml/locales_config", with <locale-config><locale android:name="en"/><locale android:name="hi"/></locale-config>. Also the Gradle androidResources { generateLocaleConfig = true } option in recent AGP (verify min AGP version).
  • Setting locales triggers a configuration change and Activity recreation. Treat it as a normal config change: state in ViewModel/saved state.
  • Server-side content/preferences (Accept-Language) must read AppCompatDelegate.getApplicationLocales(), not just Locale.getDefault().

Themed icons:

  • Provide <monochrome android:drawable="@drawable/ic_mono"/> in the adaptive icon XML. On 13 the user must enable themed icons; starting Android 16 QPR2 the system auto-themes icons without a monochrome layer (so a bad auto result is possible; add your own).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// user picks Hindi in-app (also works from system settings on 13+)
AppCompatDelegate.setApplicationLocales(LocaleListCompat.forLanguageTags("hi"))
val current = AppCompatDelegate.getApplicationLocales()   // empty list == follow system
<adaptive-icon xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android">
    <background android:drawable="@color/ic_bg"/>
    <foreground android:drawable="@drawable/ic_fg"/>
    <monochrome android:drawable="@drawable/ic_mono"/>
</adaptive-icon>

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Building your own language picker and storing Locale in SharedPreferences, so system Settings and in-app choices disagree.
  • Not listing a locale in localeConfig that you do ship translations for: it will not appear in Settings.
  • Using Locale.getDefault() in networking/formatting after the user changed per-app language in a multi-process app (each process must pick it up).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What recreates on language change? → The Activities via a locale config change; Application context resources are updated lazily, so prefer Activity context for strings.
  2. Right-to-left? → New locale may flip layout direction; use start/end attributes.
  3. Backport below 33? → AppCompat 1.6+ with the metadata service to persist; verify behavior with a non-AppCompat Activity.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE knows the feature exists. Senior wires localeConfig and the backport, treats it as a config change with state restoration, fixes Accept-Language, and checks themed-icon quality.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An app ignored per-app locale in its OkHttp Accept-Language header, so users who chose Spanish in Settings saw Spanish UI but English server-generated content.

questions.contextHtml: A food-delivery app (2.4M MAU, 55 percent on Android 13+) bumped targetSdk to 33 in release 8.2. Two weeks later Growth says push-reachable users fell from 71 percent to 38 percent among Android 13+ users, order-status engagement dropped, and support reports "I did not get my delivery update". Engineering shipped the standard permission request at first launch (after the splash). Product wants "back to 70 percent reach" and says "just ask again every launch". Legal has not weighed in. Crash rates are unchanged.
questions.promptHtml: How do you handle this, technically and as a post-incident review?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Re-prompt on every launch" or "request earlier so we capture more users". Ignores how the platform limits prompts and that denial is mostly a framing problem.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What did Android 12 users do before the change (baseline 71 percent was implicit)? What fraction denied vs never saw the dialog? Are order-critical updates also available in-app/SMS/email? Which of our pushes are transactional vs marketing? Do we measure prompt shown/accepted/denied/permanent?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Make critical order updates reach users another way (in-app order tracking, ongoing live notification via a foreground-visible UI, SMS for ETA) while permission is off. Add a Settings deep link banner for permanently denied users.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) prompt at first launch with no value context; (b) users who accepted on 12 implicitly now count as "not granted" in the metric; (c) tokens exist but notifications are blocked and our reach metric counts tokens; (d) bug in permission flow (red herring, since the crash graph is flat).
  4. How I'd verify each: Funnel events: notif_prompt_shown, granted, denied, permanent_denied; compare cohort by OS; test on Android 13 with adb shell pm revoke and fresh install; inspect NotificationManagerCompat.areNotificationsEnabled() stats; look at FCM delivery vs displayed counts.
  5. Root cause: On Android 13 notification delivery became opt-in. Pre-13 reach was free. The ask timing (before any value) produced a low accept rate, and after two denials the system will not show the dialog again.
  6. Fix: Short term: move the request to a contextual moment (after first order is placed: "Allow notifications to track your delivery"), with a pre-permission screen only for users who tapped a prime button (never block flow). Long term: tiered asks, Settings deep link for denied users, and a metric defined as areNotificationsEnabled() per user instead of token count.
fun canNotify(ctx: Context) = NotificationManagerCompat.from(ctx).areNotificationsEnabled()
  1. Prevention: Pre-release test on 13+ for every notification path; a dashboard with the funnel; a rule that new permission changes ship behind a remote flag with an experiment.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not re-prompting every launch (platform stops showing after repeat denials; users uninstall). Not tricking the user with fake system-looking dialogs. Not using SMS for marketing without consent.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Targeting 32 would have avoided this? → The system would prompt on first channel creation; control and timing are worse, not better.
  • Android 12 users upgrading to 13? → Existing installs with notifications enabled are grandfathered (verify the exact rule); new installs are opt-in.
  • Do FGS notifications count? → Hidden in the drawer when denied; still listed in the FGS Task Manager.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The "back to 71 percent" target was wrong because the old number measured delivery, not consent. Reframing the KPI as consented reach per order stage ended the argument.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: asks more often or earlier.
  • Hire: contextual ask, instrumentation, Settings deep link, non-push fallback for critical updates.
  • Strong hire: reframes the KPI, does a cohort analysis by OS and targetSdk behavior, protects user trust, and writes the post-incident review with prevention.

questions.promptHtml: What does Android 14 require for foreground services, and what failures should you expect if you get it wrong?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Foreground services are where product features meet platform policy; this question exposes real migration experience.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Targeting 34+, every foreground service must declare at least one android:foregroundServiceType in the manifest, pass a matching type (or types) to startForeground, and hold the type-specific FOREGROUND_SERVICE_<TYPE> permission plus any runtime permission the type needs (camera, microphone, location). Missing pieces throw MissingForegroundServiceTypeException or SecurityException.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Manifest: android:foregroundServiceType="location|dataSync" on the service. Base permission FOREGROUND_SERVICE remains (normal permission).
  • Type-specific permission, for example FOREGROUND_SERVICE_LOCATION, FOREGROUND_SERVICE_MEDIA_PLAYBACK, FOREGROUND_SERVICE_DATA_SYNC, FOREGROUND_SERVICE_HEALTH, etc. They are normal permissions granted at install, but their presence is checked. Some types need the runtime permission before start (for location: while-in-use location; microphone/camera similar), and 14 tightened rules for starting those from the background.
  • New types in 14: health, remoteMessaging, shortService, specialUse, systemExempted. shortService has a short timeout (about 3 minutes, verify) and cannot start other FGS types; specialUse requires a Play Console declaration and a <property> explaining the use.
  • API: ServiceCompat.startForeground(service, id, notification, type) from androidx.core 1.12+.
  • The docs say use WorkManager or user-initiated data transfer (UIDT) jobs when your use case does not match any type.

Type mismatch between manifest and the startForeground call also throws.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.FOREGROUND_SERVICE"/>
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.FOREGROUND_SERVICE_LOCATION"/>
<service android:name=".TrackingService" android:exported="false"
    android:foregroundServiceType="location"/>
class TrackingService : Service() {
    override fun onStartCommand(i: Intent?, flags: Int, startId: Int): Int {
        ServiceCompat.startForeground(
            this, NOTIF_ID, buildNotification(),
            ServiceInfo.FOREGROUND_SERVICE_TYPE_LOCATION
        )
        return START_STICKY
    }
    override fun onBind(i: Intent?) = null
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Declaring dataSync for everything. It later gets a 6h/24h timeout on 15 (Q323).
  • Calling startForeground without the runtime permission (location) and getting SecurityException.
  • Using specialUse without Play declaration, leading to review rejection.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can multiple types be combined? → Yes with |; you must hold the permission for each.
  2. When is the startForeground call due? → Within about 10 seconds after startForegroundService (ANR/ForegroundServiceDidNotStartInTimeException; verify exact timeout).
  3. Alternatives for downloading a large file? → UIDT jobs (user-initiated data transfer), or WorkManager.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE adds the attribute. Senior maps each service to the right type or a different API, handles runtime permissions and Play declarations, and anticipates the 15 timeouts.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An app shipped with mediaPlayback type for a TTS-only service; Play review flagged mismatch, and the policy fix required choosing another type or a different mechanism.

questions.promptHtml: Walk through how exact alarm permissions evolved from Android 12 to Android 14 and how you decide between SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM, USE_EXACT_ALARM, and not using exact alarms at all.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is a nuanced, policy-heavy topic where outdated knowledge produces silent feature failure.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Android 12 introduced SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM: user-grantable "Alarms & reminders" special access for exact alarms. Android 13 added USE_EXACT_ALARM, auto-granted and non-revocable but only allowed for alarm clock and calendar apps under Play policy. Android 14 stopped pre-granting SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM for newly installed apps targeting 13+ (denied by default), so I must check canScheduleExactAlarms() and handle denial. For most apps the right answer is inexact alarms, WorkManager, or setAlarmClock.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Timeline (verify the 14 default on the exact-alarm docs page):

OS Change
12 (API 31) Targeting 31: setExact* needs SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM; granted by default at install, user can revoke; revocation kills the app and cancels alarms
13 (API 33) USE_EXACT_ALARM introduced (can't be revoked; Play restricts to alarm/calendar apps); SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM no longer pre-granted for new installs targeting 33+ on 14
14 (API 34) SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM denied by default for newly installed apps targeting 33+; exceptions for updates/restores

Behavior: without permission setExact/setExactAndAllowWhileIdle throws SecurityException (targeting 31+). setAlarmClock() is exempt from the permission and shows an alarm icon; also exempt from Doze deferral. Permission changes broadcast ACTION_SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM_PERMISSION_STATE_CHANGED; on revoke, the system cancels your exact alarms, so re-schedule when granted again.

Decision framework:

  1. Is it user-visible time-of-day (alarm clock, calendar event)? -> USE_EXACT_ALARM or setAlarmClock.
  2. Is it a reminder the user set (medication, timers)? -> SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM plus a graceful degrade path.
  3. Is it "sync every 15 minutes"? -> WorkManager; never exact alarms.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val am = getSystemService(AlarmManager::class.java)
if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT < 31 || am.canScheduleExactAlarms()) {
    am.setExactAndAllowWhileIdle(AlarmManager.RTC_WAKEUP, whenMs, pi)
} else {
    // degrade: inexact window + ask user via Settings
    am.setWindow(AlarmManager.RTC_WAKEUP, whenMs, 10 * 60_000L, pi)
    startActivity(Intent(Settings.ACTION_REQUEST_SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM,
        Uri.parse("package:$packageName")))
}
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM"/>

Receiver for permission state changes should reschedule.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling canScheduleExactAlarms() once at startup and caching.
  • Declaring USE_EXACT_ALARM on a non-alarm app: Play policy violation.
  • Forgetting to re-register alarms after reboot (BOOT_COMPLETED) and after the permission is revoked/granted.
  • Using exact alarms to launch a FGS from background for sync; this is abusing the exemption (Q313).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does Doze matter here? → Inexact alarms are deferred in Doze; setExactAndAllowWhileIdle is rate-limited (roughly once per 9 minutes per app in idle, verify).
  2. What if the user revokes the permission while alarms are pending? → The system cancels exact alarms and kills the app; reschedule on grant.
  3. Alternatives for a "medicine reminder"? → setAlarmClock is valid and exempt; exact alarm permission only if shown as a clock/reminder.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE calls setExactAndAllowWhileIdle. Senior knows which permission to declare, plays the revoke/deny paths, and avoids exact alarms for sync.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An Android 14 launch where reminders silently stopped for new users: the app targeted 33, declared SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM, and never handled the default-denied state (Q321).

questions.contextHtml: A medication-reminder app (300k DAU, 62 percent Android 13 to 14) schedules daily doses with setExactAndAllowWhileIdle. Release 3.9 (targetSdk 33 to 34) went live Tuesday. By Thursday: 1-star reviews "reminder never rang", support tickets up 5x, and Crashlytics shows SecurityException: Caller com.example needs to hold android.permission.SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM or android.permission.USE_EXACT_ALARM to set exact alarms at 1.8 percent of sessions, almost all new installs on Android 14. Users who updated from 3.8 are fine. The manifest declares SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM. A teammate says "the permission is in the manifest, so it must be an OEM bug".
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose, mitigate, and fix without breaking patient trust or Play policy.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add try/catch" or "declare USE_EXACT_ALARM too". The first hides missed doses, the second risks a policy rejection if the app is not an alarm/calendar app.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
