1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which installs fail: new installs only, or updates too? (points to default-denied on 14.) Is canScheduleExactAlarms() ever checked? Which Play category and is the product strictly a clock/calendar? Do we get alarm delivery metrics (scheduled vs fired vs acknowledged)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix: check canScheduleExactAlarms(); if false, fall back to setAlarmClock (exempt from the permission and Doze-deferral, shows alarm icon) or an inexact window plus a notification, and show an in-app banner linking to the "Alarms & reminders" settings page. Server-side, push an in-app message to affected cohort (no push dependency on exact alarms).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) on 14, SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM is denied by default for new installs targeting 33+, so the call throws; (b) permission revoked later by the user; (c) Doze deferral (red herring: crash is a SecurityException, not lateness); (d) OEM battery kill (real but separate).
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce on a clean Android 14 emulator: adb shell appops get <pkg> SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM (expect deny/default); adb shell appops set <pkg> SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM allow to confirm the fix path; adb shell dumpsys alarm | grep <pkg> to inspect scheduled alarms; compare an upgrade install vs a fresh install.
  5. Root cause: Targeting 33+ and installed fresh on 14, the special access is off until the user enables it. 3.8 users kept the previously granted state; new installs did not. The code assumed "declared means granted".
  6. Fix:
fun scheduleDose(ctx: Context, atMs: Long, pi: PendingIntent) {
    val am = ctx.getSystemService(AlarmManager::class.java)
    if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT < 31 || am.canScheduleExactAlarms()) {
        am.setExactAndAllowWhileIdle(AlarmManager.RTC_WAKEUP, atMs, pi)
    } else {
        am.setAlarmClock(AlarmManager.AlarmClockInfo(atMs, showIntent(ctx)), pi) // exempt, user-visible
    }
}

Register for ACTION_SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM_PERMISSION_STATE_CHANGED to reschedule when granted; reschedule on BOOT_COMPLETED and on app update (MY_PACKAGE_REPLACED). Long term, decide with Product whether the app is an alarm app (Play policy: USE_EXACT_ALARM allowed only for alarm clock or calendar apps). 7. Prevention: Track scheduled, fired, acknowledged for alarms with permission state as a dimension; test fresh-install matrix on 12, 13, 14; lint check that every setExact* call is dominated by a permission check; a canary release to 5 percent before full rollout. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not declaring USE_EXACT_ALARM without policy fit (rejection risk). Not polling with a foreground service to "make it reliable" (battery and FGS rules). setAlarmClock shows a status bar alarm icon, which is a UX trade-off to explain to Product.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• User grants then later revokes the permission? → System cancels exact alarms and kills the app; I reschedule on the permission-state broadcast and surface a banner.
  • Can I request the permission in a dialog? → No runtime dialog; I deep-link to ACTION_REQUEST_SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM.
  • What about reminders more than 24h out? → Re-arm a rolling window with WorkManager so a lost alarm has a second chance.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The team's staging devices were all upgraded installs, which kept the old grant. The bug lived exclusively on fresh installs, i.e. exactly the acquisition cohort.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: attributes to OEM or swallows the exception.
  • Hire: checks permission state, uses fallback, deep-links settings.
  • Strong hire: separates new vs upgraded installs, knows setAlarmClock exemption and Play policy limits, adds observability and reschedule triggers.

questions.promptHtml: What does Android 15 enforce about edge-to-edge for apps targeting 35, what changes in Android 16, and how do you migrate a legacy View-based or Compose app?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the highest-impact UI change in recent targetSdk bumps; people who have done it can name concrete symptoms and fixes.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Targeting 35 on an Android 15 device, windows draw behind the status bar, navigation bar and cutout by default; the old color APIs stop having effect and content gets overlapped unless I apply insets. Android 15 had an opt-out (windowOptOutEdgeToEdgeEnforcement); targeting 36 on Android 16 disables that opt-out. The migration is: call enableEdgeToEdge(), consume WindowInsets in layouts, fix IME and system bar icon contrast.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
What changes on 15 (target 35), per the behavior-change page:

  • Status bar transparent; setStatusBarColor/R.attr#statusBarColor deprecated and no effect.
  • Gesture navigation bar transparent; 3-button navigation bar is 80 percent opaque by default, content draws behind it unless insets are applied.
  • setDecorFitsSystemWindows deprecated/disabled.
  • Display cutout: layoutInDisplayCutoutMode for non-floating windows is treated as ALWAYS (so SHORT_EDGES, NEVER, DEFAULT are interpreted as ALWAYS).
  • "Stable configuration": Configuration.screenWidthDp/heightDp no longer exclude system bars, so layout math based on them is wrong now.

Android 16 (target 36): opt-out attribute deprecated and disabled on Android 16 devices; still works for a 36-targeted app on an Android 15 device. Plan: do not rely on opt-out at all.

Insets mental model: WindowInsetsCompat types: systemBars(), displayCutout(), ime(). You either consume them in the layout system (Compose: Scaffold, windowInsetsPadding, Modifier.safeDrawingPadding()) or in Views via ViewCompat.setOnApplyWindowInsetsListener. Material 3 components handle most of the work; Material 2 and custom containers do not; RecyclerView needs padding + clipToPadding=false.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class MainActivity : ComponentActivity() {
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        enableEdgeToEdge()                      // androidx.activity 1.8+
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        setContent { AppTheme { Scaffold { padding -> Content(Modifier.padding(padding)) } } }
    }
}
// Views
ViewCompat.setOnApplyWindowInsetsListener(binding.list) { v, insets ->
    val bars = insets.getInsets(WindowInsetsCompat.Type.systemBars() or WindowInsetsCompat.Type.displayCutout())
    v.updatePadding(bottom = bars.bottom)
    insets
}
binding.list.clipToPadding = false

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Opting out via the theme attribute and shipping, then breaking on a 36-targeted build.
  • Hard-coded top/bottom margins to "fix" overlap; breaks on cutouts and 3-button vs gesture nav.
  • Dialogs, bottom sheets and splash screens (older core-splashscreen with cutout mode can crash on 15, see Q312).
  • Using Configuration.screenHeightDp for layout math.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Keyboard? → WindowInsets.ime(); use imePadding in Compose or setOnApplyWindowInsetsListener with Type.ime().
  2. System bar icon colors? → enableEdgeToEdge(SystemBarStyle...) or WindowInsetsControllerCompat.isAppearanceLightStatusBars.
  3. Does it apply below Android 15? → Enforcement is OS 15 + target 35; but enableEdgeToEdge() provides consistent behavior on older OS.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE adds paddings screen by screen. Senior migrates centrally (base Activity/theme, shared insets handling), audits low-traffic screens (onboarding, settings, dialogs), and builds screenshot tests for gesture vs 3-button nav and cutout devices.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After a 35 bump, a checkout CTA sat under the 3-button nav bar on 4 percent of devices; the screen was only tested on gesture navigation Pixels.

questions.promptHtml: What are the Android 15 foreground service timeout rules for dataSync and mediaProcessing, and which other FGS start restrictions did 15 add?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The failure mode is a crash 6 hours after launch, so people get it wrong in testing; it separates people who read the docs from those who ran it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: For apps targeting 35, dataSync and mediaProcessing foreground services get a combined budget of 6 hours in 24 hours. When it is exhausted the system calls Service.onTimeout(int, int); I have a few seconds to call stopSelf() or the app crashes with RemoteServiceException: A foreground service of type dataSync did not stop within its timeout. Starting one again after exhaustion throws ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException until the user brings the app to the foreground (which resets the timer). Also, BOOT_COMPLETED receivers cannot start several FGS types, and SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW now needs a visible overlay.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Budget is shared across all of the app's FGS of that type, not per service. Foreground bring-up resets the timer.
  • onTimeout(startId, fgsType) (API 35). After timeout, the service is no longer considered a foreground service.
  • BOOT_COMPLETED cannot launch FGS of types: dataSync, camera, mediaPlayback, phoneCall, mediaProjection, microphone (microphone already in 14). Violation: ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException.
  • SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW exemption narrowed: the app needs the permission and a visible TYPE_APPLICATION_OVERLAY window.
  • Alternatives: WorkManager for deferrable sync; UIDT jobs for user-initiated transfers; mediaProcessing type for transcoding (also 6h/24h).

Testing (works even if not targeting 35, on an Android 15 device):

adb shell am compat enable FGS_INTRODUCE_TIME_LIMITS <pkg>
adb shell device_config put activity_manager data_sync_fgs_timeout_duration 60000
adb shell am compat enable FGS_BOOT_COMPLETED_RESTRICTIONS <pkg>
adb shell am compat enable FGS_SAW_RESTRICTIONS <pkg>
adb shell am broadcast -a android.intent.action.BOOT_COMPLETED <pkg>

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class UploadService : Service() {
    override fun onTimeout(startId: Int, fgsType: Int) {   // API 35
        // persist progress, hand the rest to WorkManager, then stop
        WorkManager.getInstance(this).enqueue(OneTimeWorkRequestBuilder<UploadWorker>().build())
        stopSelf(startId)                                   // must happen within seconds
    }
    override fun onBind(i: Intent?) = null
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Implementing onTimeout but doing slow work (network, DB flush) before stopSelf.
  • Assuming the timer is per service; two services share one 6 hour budget.
  • Testing only with the app in the foreground (the user interaction resets the timer).
  • Starting a long-lived dataSync FGS at boot.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does it apply to all FGS types? → No, dataSync and mediaProcessing only (as documented). Verify the full list on the 15 FGS page when you read this.
  2. If my app is not targeting 35? → The timeout is gated on targetSdk, but compat flag lets you test early.
  3. Better design than dataSync for backups? → WorkManager with checkpoints; resume idempotently.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE knows "there is a timeout". Senior gives the 6h/24h shared budget, the timer reset, the compat flags to test, resume-safe design and the boot restrictions.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A photo-backup FGS ran "forever" overnight. After 35, crash reports showed the timeout exception between 4 and 6 hours after the app was last opened.

questions.contextHtml: A notes app (1.2M DAU) syncs large attachments through a dataSync foreground service. Release 7.0 bumps targetSdk to 35. Crashlytics on Android 15: top crash RemoteServiceException$ForegroundServiceDidNotStopInTimeException: A foreground service of type dataSync did not stop within its timeout: {com.example/.SyncService} at 0.9 percent of sessions, mostly overnight; second signal ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException: Time limit already exhausted for foreground service type dataSync at 0.4 percent. Users with big libraries (50k+ attachments) are affected. Crashes were absent in QA and staging. SyncService has a retry loop that restarts itself via startForegroundService on any failure.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose, mitigate, and re-architect.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the timeout / switch type to something else that does not time out". This is policy evasion and may fail Play review.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the service started by user action or by a boot/alarm/push? When did the last foreground visit happen before the crash? How long is a full sync for a heavy user? Is the sync resumable (cursor/checkpoints)? Do we have a server-side delta API?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship a hotfix implementing onTimeout that stops the service and schedules a WorkManager continuation. Disable the self-restart loop. Catch ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException and route to WorkManager.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) the 6h/24h shared dataSync budget gets exhausted by overnight loops; (b) the self-restart loop makes the second failure; (c) the service never calls stopSelf when idle; (d) memory kill (red herring, since the exception names timeout).
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce: am compat enable FGS_INTRODUCE_TIME_LIMITS, set data_sync_fgs_timeout_duration to 60000 ms and run a large sync; Perfetto/dumpsys activity services for how long the FGS stayed foreground; log onTimeout and elapsed time; ApplicationExitInfo for process exits.
  5. Root cause: Docs say dataSync (targeting 35) is capped at 6h per 24h shared across all dataSync services; at timeout the app has seconds to stop or the system throws. Our service ran long unattended and restarted itself, and exhaustion makes new starts throw.
  6. Fix: Short: onTimeout -> checkpoint -> enqueue WorkManager -> stopSelf. Long: user-initiated big transfer uses a user-initiated data transfer job (JobInfo.Builder.setUserInitiated(true), API 34); background sync becomes periodic/expedited WorkManager with setForeground only for user-visible progress; chunked, resumable uploads; foreground service only while the user watches progress.
override fun onTimeout(startId: Int, fgsType: Int) {
    checkpointStore.flush()                       // fast, local
    SyncScheduler.enqueueContinuation(this)       // WorkManager
    stopSelf(startId)
}
  1. Prevention: CI test that runs the service under a 30s timeout compat setup; crash alert on ForegroundService*Exception; design rule: any FGS must declare its max expected duration and resume path; avoid self-restarts.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not misusing another FGS type to dodge the limit (Play policy and runtime mismatch exceptions). WorkManager gives no hard timing guarantees; accept slower background sync for stability.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The user opens the app at 7am. What happens to the budget? → The timer resets when the app comes to the foreground.
  • Android 14 devices? → No timeout (gated on 35 and the OS 15); but FGS_INTRODUCE_TIME_LIMITS is only testable on a 15 device.
  • What if sync must be real time? → That is a push/delta design problem; use FCM high-priority plus a short expedited job, not a long FGS.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: QA never ran a sync longer than 20 minutes, so the 6-hour wall was invisible. A one-line device_config override reproduced the crash in a minute.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: increases timeouts or ignores the crash.
  • Hire: implements onTimeout, moves long work to WorkManager/UIDT.
  • Strong hire: reproduces with compat flag and device_config, kills the restart loop, designs resumable sync, and adds guardrails.

questions.promptHtml: What is the 16 KB page size change, which apps does it actually break, and how do you check and fix an app that includes native libraries?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is an ecosystem-wide deadline-driven change; seniors must scope the real risk (native code, third-party SDKs) instead of panicking or ignoring it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Since Android 15, AOSP supports devices whose kernel uses 16 KB memory pages instead of 4 KB. Pure Kotlin/Java apps are fine. Apps with native code (my own NDK code or SDK .so files) must have ELF segments aligned to 16 KB and, if libraries are stored uncompressed, 16 KB zip-aligned; otherwise they crash at load or fail to install. Play requires apps targeting 35+ to support 16 KB on 64-bit devices.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Memory is managed in pages; a 16 KB kernel maps in 16 KB units. Native libraries with LOAD segments aligned to 4 KB cannot be mapped correctly. Code that hard-codes 4096 or uses PAGE_SIZE breaks (use getpagesize() or sysconf(_SC_PAGESIZE)).
  • Toolchain: AGP 8.5.1+ for zip alignment of uncompressed libraries; NDK r28+ compiles 16 KB aligned by default; for NDK r27 and below add -Wl,-z,max-page-size=16384 (and common-page-size).
  • Failure modes (from the docs): RELRO segment not 16 KB aligned causes segmentation fault at runtime on NDK r27 and lower without flags; a bundle with 4 KB zip alignment may fail to install.
  • Android 16 added compatibility mode: on a 16 KB device, if the package manager sees 4 KB-aligned ELF + 4 KB zip alignment it runs in compat mode and shows a one-time dialog; android:pageSizeCompat in the manifest controls this. It is a bridge, not a fix.
  • Play deadline: the page I read states that after a given 2027 date app updates that do not support 16 KB will not be releasable; earlier dates were announced and extended, so check Play Console for current dates (verify).
  • Custom allocators (jemalloc, game engines) can inflate RSS on 16 KB; docs give guidance on release thresholds and dense-first allocation.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
# Is the device 16 KB?
adb shell getconf PAGE_SIZE            # 16384 expected

# ELF alignment check per library
llvm-objdump -p libfoo.so | grep LOAD  # align must be 2**14 or higher

# zip alignment
zipalign -c -P 16 -v 4 app.apk         # "Verification successful"
bundletool dump config --bundle=app.aab | grep alignment  # PAGE_ALIGNMENT_16K
// build.gradle.kts: legacy fallback only if you cannot upgrade AGP
android { packaging { jniLibs { useLegacyPackaging = true } } }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming "we have no NDK" while an analytics/ads/ML SDK ships .so files.
  • Fixing only your .so but not prebuilts or libc++_shared.so from an old NDK.
  • Relying on the compat mode dialog as the final state; users see a warning and performance is not the same.
  • Testing only on x86 emulator without a 16 KB image.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you find offenders fast? → APK Analyzer lib/ view with alignment column; Android Studio lint; check_elf_alignment.sh.
  2. Does it matter if I only ship armeabi-v7a? → The Play requirement covers 64-bit; 32-bit-only libs have different constraints; verify current policy.
  3. Why do 16 KB devices exist? → Better launch times and power under memory pressure (docs cite ~3.16 percent faster launch on average); costs slightly more memory.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "rebuild NDK". Senior scopes via APK Analyzer, owns SDK vendor follow-up, defines CI checks (zipalign + ELF alignment), plans an emulator/device test pass, and handles allocator behavior.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A game shipped a 3rd-party anti-cheat .so built at 4 KB alignment. It ran in compat mode on Pixel 16 KB builds and crashed on a device without compat, found only after a Play pre-launch report.

questions.contextHtml: A fintech app (4M MAU, arm64 only in practice) ships 11 native libraries: 2 are ours (C++ crypto, built with NDK r25), 9 come from SDKs (analytics, payments, a face-liveness vendor, video player, crash reporter). The Play Console shows a warning that app updates must support 16 KB page sizes. Product wants to ship a feature release in 3 weeks. AGP is 8.2, useLegacyPackaging is false, the face-liveness vendor says "16 KB support coming Q3", and QA has no 16 KB device. On an Android 16 beta device with a 16 KB kernel, the app launches but shows the page-size compatibility dialog.
questions.promptHtml: Plan the work, sequence risks, and tell Product what you will and will not promise.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "We have a dialog but the app runs, so ignore until Play forces us" or "recompile everything in NDK r28 this sprint" without knowing which libraries are third-party.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the Play date for our targetSdk and release track? Which SDKs have 16 KB builds already? Can the liveness feature be remotely disabled or loaded as a dynamic feature? What fraction of users is on devices likely to have 16 KB kernels (small now, growing)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Mitigation is mostly risk containment: confirm the compat dialog is the worst-case user impact on 16 KB devices today, add android:pageSizeCompat decisions deliberately, and ensure Android 15 16 KB devices are not crashing (compat mode exists on 16+; on 15 behavior depends on the build, verify).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (what could fail): (a) 4 KB-aligned .so from SDKs; (b) our own libs on NDK r25 without alignment flags; (c) zip alignment when building the AAB with AGP 8.2; (d) hard-coded 4096 in our crypto code; (e) allocator or mmap assumptions.
  4. How I'd verify each: APK Analyzer alignment column for every .so; llvm-objdump -p lib.so | grep LOAD for align 2**14; zipalign -c -P 16 -v 4 on the universal APK from the bundle; bundletool dump config for PAGE_ALIGNMENT_16K; boot the 16 KB emulator image or a Pixel with the "Boot with 16KB page size" developer option; adb shell getconf PAGE_SIZE; grep our C++ for PAGE_SIZE, 4096, mmap.
  5. Root cause (of risk): AGP and NDK vintage plus unknown SDK builds. Native code compiled before r28 is typically 4 KB aligned; unaligned RELRO can segfault at load; unaligned zip layout can block installs.
  6. Fix: Week 1: inventory and upgrade AGP to 8.5.1+, NDK to r28+ (or add -Wl,-z,max-page-size=16384 -Wl,-z,common-page-size=16384 on r27 and below), rebuild our two libs, replace PAGE_SIZE with sysconf(_SC_PAGESIZE). Week 1-2: bump each SDK to its 16 KB-aligned version; file vendor tickets with dates. Week 2-3: CI gate that fails the build on any .so with LOAD alignment < 2**14 or failed zipalign -P 16; run smoke tests on a 16 KB emulator. Liveness vendor: ship behind a remote flag; if their build slips, decide between a fallback vendor or delayed enablement.
  7. Prevention: The CI gate; a quarterly SDK audit; an "NDK/AGP minimum" doc; Play pre-launch report review.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not relying on compat mode as the plan (the dialog degrades trust in a fintech app and it is a stopgap). Not forcing useLegacyPackaging=true as the fix: it bloats install size and risks install failures on low-storage devices. I'd promise Product: our code and 8 of 9 SDKs aligned and gated in 3 weeks; the liveness feature depends on the vendor, with a flagged fallback.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Vendor refuses to ship a fix? → Replace the vendor, or isolate the feature (dynamic feature module/optional) so it does not block release; Play's requirement applies to the whole app.
  • Perf regression on 16 KB? → Memory use is slightly higher; custom allocators need dense-first allocation and dynamic purge thresholds.
  • Does x86_64 matter? → The Play rule is for 64-bit; ensure both arm64-v8a and x86_64 are aligned if shipped (the docs' check script covers both).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: One tiny prebuilt libc++_shared.so from an old NDK was the only unaligned file in an otherwise clean build. The CI gate found it in 20 seconds; manual review had missed it for weeks.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: ignores or says "Kotlin only so fine".
  • Hire: inventories libs, upgrades AGP/NDK, checks alignment, tests on a 16 KB environment.
  • Strong hire: adds CI gates, vendor strategy with flagged fallback, communicates scoped promises, understands compat mode as a bridge.

questions.contextHtml:
A support-chat app bumps targetSdk to 36. On Android 16 devices, QA reports: (1) pressing back on the chat screen with an unsent draft no longer shows the "Discard draft?" dialog and the draft is lost; (2) the system back-to-home animation plays for a screen that must confirm first; (3) the custom BackHandler in a Compose bottom sheet works but the legacy View screen does not. On Android 14 with targetSdk 36 everything still worked. Code:

class ChatActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    override fun onBackPressed() {
        if (viewModel.hasDraft) showDiscardDialog() else super.onBackPressed()
    }
    override fun onKeyDown(keyCode: Int, event: KeyEvent?): Boolean {
        if (keyCode == KeyEvent.KEYCODE_BACK && viewModel.hasDraft) { showDiscardDialog(); return true }
        return super.onKeyDown(keyCode, event)
    }
}

The manifest has no enableOnBackInvokedCallback attribute.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the bug and fix it for 36, keeping pre-36 devices working.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Set enableOnBackInvokedCallback=false" as the permanent fix, or "override onBackPressed harder". Both fail the migration.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which screens intercept back? Fragments with FragmentManager back stack? Any use of onKeyDown/dispatchKeyEvent for back? Which third-party libraries (nav, dialogs, WebView) override back?
  2. Immediate mitigation: The doc-supported temporary opt-out: android:enableOnBackInvokedCallback="false" on <application> or the <activity>. That restores the old onBackPressed path while I migrate. It is a bridge, not a plan.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) for apps targeting 36 on Android 16, predictive back system animations are on by default and onBackPressed is not called and KEYCODE_BACK is not dispatched; (b) the Compose BackHandler works since it registers an OnBackInvokedCallback via OnBackPressedDispatcher; (c) third-party views doing key handling (red herring until verified).
  4. How I'd verify each: Run the same build on an Android 14 and Android 16 device; breakpoints in onBackPressed/onKeyDown (never hit on 16); adb shell dumpsys window for registered back callbacks (verify); developer option for predictive back animations exists on earlier releases for testing.
  5. Root cause: The app uses legacy back interception APIs. The 36-target platform behavior does not call them. Compose's BackHandler already used the supported path, so it still works.
  6. Fix: Use OnBackPressedDispatcher with an OnBackPressedCallback whose isEnabled reflects state; remove onBackPressed/onKeyDown. Enable the callback only while a draft exists so the system animation remains for normal screens.
class ChatActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    private val backCallback = object : OnBackPressedCallback(false) {
        override fun handleOnBackPressed() { showDiscardDialog() }
    }
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        onBackPressedDispatcher.addCallback(this, backCallback)
        lifecycleScope.launch {
            repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
                viewModel.hasDraft.collect { backCallback.isEnabled = it }
            }
        }
    }
}

For animated custom transitions use PredictiveBackHandler in Compose (activity-compose 1.8+) or OnBackAnimationCallback on 34+ (verify exact API level). 7. Prevention: Lint/grep ban on onBackPressed overrides; instrumented test with pressBack() on an API 36 emulator; screenshot test for the cross-activity transition. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not leaving the opt-out in place indefinitely (docs describe it as temporary). Not always-enabled callbacks, which disable the system back-to-home animation for every screen.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Android 16 but targetSdk 34? → Old behavior; predictive back stays opt-in via the manifest attribute.
  • Fragments? → FragmentManager back stack integrates with the dispatcher; animations need Fragment 1.7+ and AndroidX transitions (verify versions).
  • 3-button navigation? → Android 16 supports predictive back for properly migrated apps via long-press back.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The draft-loss bug was found on day one of beta only because an engineer happened to use a Pixel on the beta channel. The suite had no API 36 emulator.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: edits onBackPressed or sets the opt-out forever.
  • Hire: migrates to OnBackPressedCallback and knows the 36 gate.
  • Strong hire: toggles callback state to preserve system animations, covers fragments/Compose/3-button, and adds tests.

questions.promptHtml: What does Android 16 change about screen orientation and resizability restrictions, who is affected, and how do you prepare?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Foldables and tablets are a growing share; portrait-locked apps are still common. It tests UI state discipline and platform awareness.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: For apps targeting 36 on displays with smallest width >= 600dp, the system ignores screenOrientation, resizableActivity, minAspectRatio, maxAspectRatio, and setRequestedOrientation() locks: the app fills the window and can rotate or be resized. Exceptions: games (appCategory), user opt-in to the app's default behavior, and screens smaller than sw600dp. There is a temporary opt-out through a manifest property, and it will not apply when targeting 37.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Ignored values include portrait/landscape variants (reverse, sensor, user). The change is about large screens only; phones are unchanged.
  • Consequences: more configuration changes -> Activity recreation -> lost state if you lean on onSaveInstanceState/ViewModel poorly. Layouts designed for portrait stretch. Animations and Display assumptions break.
  • Opt-out (temporary, per activity or per app): android.window.PROPERTY_COMPAT_ALLOW_RESTRICTED_RESIZABILITY = true. Result is the old compat mode (letterboxing). Not available when targeting 37.
  • Testing: adb shell am compat enable UNIVERSAL_RESIZABLE_BY_DEFAULT <pkg>; tablet/foldable emulators; resizable emulator.
  • Build adaptivity with window size classes (WindowSizeClass / material3-adaptive), ListDetailPaneScaffold, WindowInfoTracker for folds, and avoid Configuration.orientation as a layout switch.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
<!-- temporary opt-out, per activity -->
<activity android:name=".LegacyActivity" android:exported="false">
    <property android:name="android.window.PROPERTY_COMPAT_ALLOW_RESTRICTED_RESIZABILITY"
              android:value="true"/>
</activity>
val windowSizeClass = currentWindowAdaptiveInfo().windowSizeClass
val twoPane = windowSizeClass.windowWidthSizeClass != WindowWidthSizeClass.COMPACT

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using the opt-out as the product decision; it is time-limited.
  • Handling rotation with android:configChanges to avoid recreation, then breaking multi-window resizing.
  • Camera/video apps assuming sensor orientation = display orientation.
  • Treating "tablet" as a device model rather than a window size (windows resize on desktop mode).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why exempt games? → They declare appCategory=game and often depend on fixed orientation.
  2. How does the user force old behavior? → Through the device's aspect ratio settings (documented exception).
  3. How to keep state through resize? → ViewModel + rememberSaveable/saved state; avoid recreating expensive objects per config.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "tablets will rotate now". Senior maps the exact attributes, exceptions and the 37 sunset, plans state restoration and adaptive layouts, and sets up compat-flag testing.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A portrait-only video app targeting 36 showed black bars-free stretched video and overlapped controls on a foldable inner display, and users lost a half-filled form on rotation.

questions.promptHtml: What changes in Android 16 affect background work (JobScheduler quota, scheduled executors, broadcasts), and which of them apply to all apps versus only apps targeting 36?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Background-work changes cause silent behavior shifts, not crashes. Seniors know which ones hit them without a targetSdk bump.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Several are all-apps: JobScheduler runtime quota (regular and expedited) now depends on app standby bucket, whether the job started while the app was top, and whether it runs concurrently with a foreground service; setImportantWhileForeground is a no-op; ordered broadcast priority is only honored within a process; abandoned jobs get a new stop reason. One is target-36 only: ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor.scheduleAtFixedRate runs at most one missed execution on return to a valid lifecycle.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
From the 16 behavior-change pages:

Change Scope Notes
JobScheduler quota tweaks All apps on 16 WorkManager, JobScheduler, DownloadManager affected
Jobs started while app top, continuing after invisible All apps adhere to runtime quota
Jobs concurrent with a FGS All apps adhere to quota; use UIDT for user-initiated transfers
STOP_REASON_TIMEOUT_ABANDONED All apps if JobParameters is GC'd without jobFinished
setImportantWhileForeground All apps ignored; isImportantWhileForeground() returns false
Ordered broadcast priority All apps respected only within app process; range confined to (SYSTEM_LOW+1, SYSTEM_HIGH-1)
scheduleAtFixedRate catch-up Target 36 at most one missed run executes

Operational implications: log WorkInfo.getStopReason() / JobParameters.getStopReason(); use JobScheduler#getPendingJobReasonsHistory (API 36) to understand why jobs did not run. WorkManager hides JobParameters, so abandoned-job issues hit hand-rolled JobServices.

Testing:

adb shell am compat enable OVERRIDE_QUOTA_ENFORCEMENT_TO_TOP_STARTED_JOBS <pkg>
adb shell am compat enable OVERRIDE_QUOTA_ENFORCEMENT_TO_FGS_JOBS <pkg>
adb shell am set-standby-bucket <pkg> rare
adb shell am get-standby-bucket <pkg>
adb shell am compat enable STPE_SKIP_MULTIPLE_MISSED_PERIODIC_TASKS <pkg>

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class SyncWorker(ctx: Context, p: WorkerParameters) : CoroutineWorker(ctx, p) {
    override suspend fun doWork(): Result = try { syncAll(); Result.success() } catch (e: CancellationException) {
        Log.w("Sync", "stopped reason=${if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 31) stopReason else -1}")
        throw e
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Holding a job open from a foreground UI session (top-started) and expecting it to finish later without quota.
  • Cross-process receivers relying on android:priority to order each other's handling.
  • Hand-written JobService keeping no strong reference to JobParameters.
  • Assuming the ScheduledExecutor change applies without bumping targetSdk (it does not).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you reproduce a quota-stopped job? → Put the app in rare bucket with am set-standby-bucket, run a long job, read the stop reason.
  2. What replaces ordered broadcasts across processes? → An explicit coordination channel (bound service, ContentProvider, shared DB), not priority.
  3. Why would a periodic timer "burst" before 36? → Missed fixed-rate executions all fire at once on resume; 36 fixes to one.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "use WorkManager". Senior separates all-apps from target-gated, instruments stop reasons, and uses bucket overrides to test.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After an Android 16 rollout, nightly uploads in apps that kept a foreground service alive ran short; jobs concurrent with the FGS hit quota, which WorkManager stop-reason logging made visible.

questions.contextHtml: A marketplace app (6M MAU, targetSdk 33, 480 Gradle modules-equivalent codebase, 40 percent legacy View screens, 9 third-party SDKs) must reach targetSdk 36 before the Play deadline in 10 weeks. Last year's 33 bump caused two incidents (a crash cluster from notification handling and a login regression). The org wants a plan, a risk ranking, and a rollout that will not cause an incident. Crash-free sessions today: 99.62 percent, ANR 0.21 percent.
questions.promptHtml: Lay out your targetSdk bump playbook from 33 to 36 and how you will test behavior changes with compat flags.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Change the number, fix compile errors, run regression, ship". It skips reading three releases of docs, all-apps changes, and staged rollout.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Hard Play deadline and whether it applies to updates only? Is it allowed to bump in two steps (34 then 36)? Which SDKs have 34/35/36-ready versions? Which screens are revenue-critical? What is our canary capability (staged rollout %, feature flags)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not applicable; this is planned work. I would, however, start with compileSdk 36 and keep targetSdk 33 in a tracking branch to see compile and lint errors early without runtime change.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (what will bite): (a) 34: FGS types + permissions, receiver export flags, implicit intents to non-exported components, mutable implicit PendingIntents, exact alarm default denial, JobScheduler main thread ANR; (b) 35: edge-to-edge, FGS timeouts, BOOT_COMPLETED limits, 16 KB for native SDKs; (c) 36: edge-to-edge opt-out gone, predictive back default, large-screen orientation ignored, scheduleAtFixedRate change; (d) all-apps changes arriving with OS updates regardless of target.
  4. How I'd verify each: Create a checklist from the "targeting N" and "all apps" pages for 34, 35, 36. For each item: lint/grep rule, a compat-flag test, an owner. Use adb shell am compat enable|disable|reset <CHANGE_ID> <pkg> on debuggable builds on a matching-OS device; adb shell dumpsys platform_compat to list change IDs; Developer options -> App Compatibility Changes. Known IDs from the docs: FGS_INTRODUCE_TIME_LIMITS, FGS_BOOT_COMPLETED_RESTRICTIONS, FGS_SAW_RESTRICTIONS, REQUIRE_EXACT_ALARM_PERMISSION, NOTIFICATION_TRAMPOLINE_BLOCK, UNIVERSAL_RESIZABLE_BY_DEFAULT, STPE_SKIP_MULTIPLE_MISSED_PERIODIC_TASKS, OVERRIDE_QUOTA_ENFORCEMENT_TO_*.
  5. Root cause of past incidents: Bumps were done as a single number change by one engineer, after reading only the headline features; no per-item owner and no canary.
  6. Fix (the plan):
    • Weeks 1-2: inventory + dependency upgrades (AGP, SDKs, AndroidX); 16 KB alignment audit; lint warnings to errors for UnspecifiedImmutableFlag, UnspecifiedRegisterReceiverFlag, ExportedReceiver.
    • Weeks 2-5: bump to 34 first (ship it), then 35, then 36, each as its own release train. Smaller blast radius, bisectable.
    • Per step: UI screenshot tests on gesture vs 3-button nav, cutout, tablet size class; FGS inventory with types and permissions; alarm/permission matrix; instrumented tests on API 34/35/36 emulators; compat flags to test 36 behaviors on a 35 device where flags exist.
    • Weeks 6-9: staged rollout 1 -> 5 -> 20 -> 50 -> 100 percent with automatic halt if crash-free drops > 0.1 pp or ANR > 0.3 percent; remote flags for risky features (e.g., FGS paths).
    • Week 10: buffer; keep temporary opt-outs (predictive back attribute, large-screen resize property) documented with expiry tickets because they are temporary by design.
  7. Prevention: A reusable "behavior-change checklist" template per Android release; a yearly OS-beta testing slot (developer preview devices in CI); Play pre-launch reports; subscribe to Android developer blog and read both lists each release.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not jumping three levels in one release. Not using every opt-out to hit the date, because opt-outs carry their own deadlines (large-screen opt-out ends at target 37; edge-to-edge opt-out ends at 36). Not skipping all-apps changes just because they don't depend on targetSdk.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Leadership asks for a 2-week version. → Ship targetSdk 34 only if Play allows, with 35/36 as a follow-up; refuse to bundle 35/36 changes with 16 KB risk unaudited.
  • A vendor SDK breaks on 36. → Feature-flag the SDK path, pin a fallback version, escalate; fixing app code around an SDK bug is the last resort.
  • How do you know it worked? → Crash-free, ANR and key-flow success metrics by OS and targetSdk cohort, compared to a control from the previous release.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The previous bump's login regression came from an implicit intent to a non-exported activity that only a marketing deep-link path used. A per-item behavior-change checklist with an owner would have flagged that exact API in review.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: changes the number and fixes compile errors.
  • Hire: reads release notes per level, stages bumps, uses lint and tests, stages the rollout.
  • Strong hire: builds the checklist per all-apps and target-gated changes, uses compat flags and bucket/device_config overrides, tracks opt-out expiry, and defines rollout halt criteria with metrics.
